title: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is set by the separation between observed large-scale and uncontrollable small-scale features.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So the idea that randomness comes purely from initial conditions can be realistic only for a fairly small number of steps; randomness which is seen after that must therefore typically be attributed to other mechanisms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “Chaos Theory and Randomness from Initial Conditions” (from p. 304), p. 310. Scope: physical systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing records and simulations can test selected chaotic systems and estimate finite predictability horizons. They do not support the broad physical generalization or the specific pegboard scale without richer controlled measurements.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For specified chaotic apparatuses, combine measured initial-state precision and environmental-noise spectra with validated dynamical models to compute the predictability horizon and the scale reached by amplified uncertainty. Test whether initial uncertainty dominates only for roughly the stated number of collisions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public data rarely record microscopic initial conditions and environmental perturbations together.

The horizon is apparatus- and precision-dependent.

Attribution after divergence is model-dependent.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The quantitative core is an amplification count from public atomic and thermal scales, and a doubling map reaches atomic lengths in a few tens of steps, which a small team can recompute. Raw trajectories of the pegboard, kneading, and mirror devices are not a public dataset, so the laboratory half is a scaling argument rather than a reanalysis of runs. Around ten and typically remain order-of-magnitude statements tied to apparatus size.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Count e-foldings between a stated macroscopic tolerance and an atomic or thermal scale, using a doubling per collision or per kneading step. A result of order ten collisions for a laboratory-scale pegboard would support that clause; a separation of hundreds of collisions would challenge it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A real pegboard also has fabrication error, not only atomic uncertainty.

Kneading and mirror arrangements are idealized, so only the scale-separation arithmetic is directly calculable.

Around ten depends on the size of the apparatus and the initial uncertainty.
